items.title: Louis Keppard Interview, 1961-01-19
items.q: That's me on the guitar, Lloyd Kephart. There's Johnny, I mean there's Eric Garland on bass.

ctx.x: If you could tell us about some of the men on this picture.

You see now this here, this picture here, her husband is on this photograph, is her husband is the manager of the shore. Now she is black enough to impotate. She was a white person. She's a white person but she's black enough. This is nothing but a drop scenery but it's in Chicago, Illinois. That's during 1917. Now she's black enough to entertain. She's the dancer. Now her husband is the manager of the show. He's what they call a booking agent. That's her husband. And now the violin, he's leading the band. That's…
To get back to Dewey, was he working here in town? Was he working here?

items.title: Ed Garland Interview, 1958-08-08; 1958-09-03
items.q: Then I, then I left and I was taking the group. I was taking Sugar Johnny. Trumpet. Trumpet. Lewis Kepert, guitar. Myself on bass.

ctx.x: You remember that? The first time the first bunch went away was Freddie, George Dibacque, Jimmy Pollard, a bunch like that. Eddie Benson. Eddie Benson went off to the next group. Who else went? Another group went because they're taking Cantrell. Another group went was Cantrell, Eddie Atkins. Yeah, that's right. And Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez, yeah, that's it. And Frankie Hain. Frankie Hain. And Teo. Lorraine Teo. Who was the Teo? Lil Cantrell. That's right. Then I, then I left and I was taking the group. I was…
It was the trombone. Huh? The trombone. You remember?

items.title: Ed Garland Interview, 1957-04-16
items.q: I brought Sugar Johnny, trumpet, Louis Keppert on guitar, Roy Palmer on trombone, Herbert Lindsay on violin, and a boy named Lawrence Duell on clarinet, myself on bass.

ctx.x: No. Mabel Elaine and her jazz band. She's a white girl. She used to clunk band. You know how Boa Jingles used to dance with wooden shoes on. She had the same thing. She used to be in a bale of cotton. She was blackface. When you get on the stage, that bale of cotton was out there. They couldn't go out. We'd be all lying around in this cotton, see, with a couple of holes on, satin cover holes, different colors, and bandana, hangers, and hats. So I had, when we started playing, this fave of cotton opened up. And…
